title: RoboWits: Unexpected Challenges for Robotic Creative Problem Solving
claim: Standard agents repeat direct but infeasible actions as difficulty escalates; an ideal agent reasons through failures to find creative recovery strategies.
layout: 3 dashed panels around central instruction box, escalating difficulty, robot vs ideal-robot columns
description: The figure shows one shared instruction in a central yellow box: retrieve the cube from the container and place it on the green target area. A 'Robot vs. Ideal Robot' icon pair sits above it. Three dashed rounded panels, Easy (top-left), Hard (bottom-left) and Harder (right), show increasing difficulty with small blurred scene thumbnails. Each panel has robot icons with thought bubbles and filmstrips of real bimanual robot frames. The standard robot's bubble says 'Pick the cube…' and ends in a red X. The ideal robot's bubble reasons, for example 'Narrow open, can't pick… Grasp the cup and pour out the cube…', and ends in a green check. Red and blue text highlight failures and new strategies. Down-arrows link the sequential attempts. The eye goes first to the central instruction and the red X and green check marks.
caption: Creative problem solving under unexpected challenges. The figure contrasts the reasoning and execution processes of a standard robot (left) and an ideal robot (right) performing tasks under the same instruction but escalating difficulty. While both succeed in an Easy setting (top-left), the standard robot gets stuck repeating direct but unfeasible actions when the cube is trapped deep inside a cup (Hard, bottom-left), or when the cup is firmly affixed to the table (Harder, right). In contrast, an ideal robot demonstrates true creative problem-solving by actively reasoning through unexpected failures to dynamically discover and execute novel recovery strategies.
abstract: The ability to reason, adapt, and creatively solve problems under unexpected challenges is essential for robots operating in real-world environments. However, current robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize skill-level execution and provide limited insight into such cognitive reasoning capabilities. We introduce RoboWits, a bi-manual robotic benchmark designed to systematically evaluate cognitive reasoning, creative tool use, and robustness to unexpected conditions. To enable scalable construction of high-quality reasoning-centric unexpected scenarios, we propose an automated task generation pipeline formulated as a multi-agent cooperative framework, comprising agents for seed task generation and verification, metric generation, scene generation, and task mutation. Using the pipeline, we curated 30 diverse seed tasks and 200 tasks with mutations and graded difficulty across geometry, material, and assembly-based reasoning. We benchmark popular robot policies, pre-trained VLAs, a zero-shot policy built on a frontier VLM, and oracle-state planners. Our results reveal a significant performance gap: while pre-trained VLAs exhibit preliminary success on seed tasks after fine-tuning, they struggle to perform on mutated tasks, implying their brittleness in manipulation tasks requiring reasoning, strategy adaptation, and robustness to deceptive or constrained environments. A zero-shot policy built on GPT-6 Astra outperforms all fine-tuned VLAs, yet still loses about a fifth of its success on mutated tasks, showing that stronger foundation models alone do not close the robustness gap. See our project page https://umass-embodied-agi.github.io/RoboWits/ for videos.
